comments.author: Alexander Terp
comments.body:
Measured while reviewing: frame.decode reads 1.76 ns/byte here against a baseline of 0.83, which trips the 2.00x tolerance and makes ./dev --perf red before anybody changes anything. frame.vt_parse reads 5.72 against its own baseline without tripping, so the whole table looks shifted rather than one entry being wrong - consistent with the baseline having been recorded on a different machine rather than with a real regression.

Also confirmed from the same run: roster.build is measured and printed as 'new... nothing gates it yet' because perf/baseline.json has no entry for it. Comparison::is_clean() only fails on regressions and missing entries, not unbaselined ones, so that cost cannot fail a run today - and it is the per-title-change, per-pane cost architecture.md names as the one worth watching. Whatever re-records the baseline should pick it up.

Not re-recorded here: the machine was busy with the review, and choosing what a baseline describes is a call worth making deliberately.

comments.author: Alexander Terp
comments.body:
**Three causes, separated by measurement, and the ~2x is not one of them.**

**The clock resolved a microsecond, and that is provable from the file itself.** Multiply any
recorded cost by its own unit count and you get a whole number of microseconds, with no
exceptions: `input.encode` 35.0 x 400 = 14,000 ns, `view.build` 118.67 x 3,000 = 356,000 ns,
`seam.dispatch` 290 x 100 = 29,000 ns. The harness timed through `muster_core`'s
`monotonic_now`, and `clock_getres(CLOCK_MONOTONIC)` returns exactly 1e-06 on this machine
against 4.2e-08 for `CLOCK_UPTIME_RAW`.

`pane.encoder` is the one this ruined. Its whole iteration was 1,000 ns - a single tick - so
its 66.67 ns/pane was the clock's resolution over fifteen panes and nothing about the encoder.
It could only ever read 66.67, 133.3 or 200, and a 2.00x tolerance on a quantity that steps by
100% gates nothing. Fixed, and it now does twenty windows' worth per iteration.

**But the clock is not the ~2x.** Measured both ways on one unchanged tree: the two clocks
agree on every benchmark to within noise. This card's "looks more like a timer" instinct was
right about a real defect and wrong about which symptom it caused.

**The baseline measured a workload that has since changed, and nothing said so.**
`recorded_frame_streams` globs every `corpus/*/*/frames.ndjson` and concatenates them, so
`frame.decode` and `frame.vt_parse` replay whatever is in the corpus that day. Solving
`0.8304517112750838 x n = 122,000` gives n = 146,908 bytes, which is exactly the corpus at
`b5daf00`, the commit that recorded the baseline. Today it is 197,609 - `dc276cd` added the
Linux frame-fidelity capture on 2026-08-17. A third more input, judged against a rate measured
over the old one, with no signal anywhere.

**Build flags are ruled out.** `--perf` builds `--release` always, `[profile.release]` sets only
`debug = "line-tables-only"` and landed at `986e65a` on 2026-08-13, nine hours *before* the
baseline was recorded. `f571cd7` touched `[profile.dev]` only. `.cargo/config.toml` carries no
codegen flags, and libghostty-vt is built `-Doptimize=ReleaseFast`.

**The baseline still describes this machine.** Eight consecutive runs of the current tree, at a
load average of about ten:

    benchmark              min       max   spread   baseline
    frame.decode          0.79      0.83    1.05x   0.83
    frame.vt_parse        3.61      3.78    1.05x   3.79
    input.encode          33.8      38.5    1.14x   35.0
    mirror.apply           233       248    1.06x   228
    seam.dispatch          293       318    1.09x   290
    view.build             137       150    1.09x   118.7
    roster.build           255       270    1.06x   unbaselined
    pane.channel         90,128   127,806    1.42x   86,400
    pane.encoder          51.9      65.7    1.27x   66.67 (fictitious)

So the ~2x has not reproduced, on a machine busier than the one that produced it. Whatever the
2026-08-16 run measured was a transient state of this laptop, not a property of the code or the
harness - which is the answer to "do not just re-record": there is nothing here to re-record
*for*. The tier reads green against the 2026-08-13 file today.

**The tolerance was the wrong shape, and now there is a number behind saying so.** The six
arithmetic-over-a-buffer benchmarks vary by at most 1.14x run to run even at load ten; the two
that touch the OS vary by 1.27x and 1.42x. A single 2.00x covered the noisiest and left the
quiet ones ungated - a change doubling the cost of every byte Muster reads passed. Tolerance is
now per cost and lives in the baseline file: 1.5x default, 2.0x for `pane.encoder`, 3.0x for
`pane.channel`. They only take effect once a baseline is written with them.

**One drift that is real and is not the machine.** `view.build` reads 137-150 against a
baseline of 118.7, consistently across all eight runs. `view_cost()` has changed since the
baseline was recorded - `View::of` gained four closures and `full_window` now puts an agent and
a title on every pane - so it is measuring more work than its baseline number describes. The
unit count is unchanged at 3,000, so the workload guard cannot see it. Worth a look on its own
rather than being swept into a re-record.

creator: Alexander Terp
description:
`./dev --perf` fails on an unchanged tree. Measured 2026-08-16: with the working tree stashed, `frame.decode` reports 1.84 ns/byte against a baseline of 0.83 (2.22x, tolerance 2.00x), and every other benchmark is up by a similar factor - `input.encode` 35 to 57.5, `mirror.apply` 228 to 326, `frame.vt_parse` 3.79 to 5.70. Nothing on those paths has changed; the numbers were recorded 2026-08-13 and the failure reproduces with no diff at all.

So the tier currently cannot tell a regression from the machine, which is worse than not having it: a real regression now lands in a run that was already red.

**Do not just re-record.** `./dev --perf --record` would bake in whatever this machine is doing today, and if the cause is thermal or load then tomorrow's baseline is wrong in the other direction. Worth finding out which it is first:

- Whether it reproduces on an idle machine, cold, with nothing else running - six herdr daemons and a browser were up when this was measured.
- Whether the harness is measuring what it thinks it is. A uniform ~2x across four unrelated benchmarks looks more like a timer, a build flag or CPU frequency scaling than like four independent slowdowns.
- Whether the baseline needs a per-machine dimension at all. It already records `machine` and `recorded`; what it does not record is whether the machine was quiet, which is the variable that appears to matter.

Also worth deciding whether the tolerance is the right shape. 2.00x on a benchmark whose absolute cost is under a nanosecond per byte is a tight ratio on a small number, and a fixed ratio treats `frame.decode` and `pane.channel` (85 microseconds per pane) as equally noisy when they cannot be.

Found while checking that the config-reload work had not slowed the keystroke path. It had not - `input.encode` was faster with the change than without it on the same run - but establishing that took three runs and a stash, which is the cost this card is about.

Adjacent: a_28UsunMWa, the perf tier failing after the ssh tier.
title: 📉 The perf baseline no longer describes this machine
